content.text:
Earlier, you have studied different types of polynomials. One type was the quadratic polynomial of the form ax² + bx + c, a ≠ 0. When we equate this polynomial to zero, we get a quadratic equation. Quadratic equations come up when we deal with many real-life situations. For instance, suppose a charity trust decides to build a prayer hall having a carpet area of 300 square metres with its length one metre more than twice its breadth. What should be the length and breadth of the hall?
Suppose the breadth of the hall is x metres. Then, its length should be (2x + 1) metres. We can depict this information pictorially.
Now,    area of the hall = (2x + 1). x m² = (2x² + x) m²
So,    2x² + x = 300    (Given)
Therefore,    2x² + x - 300 = 0
So, the breadth of the hall should satisfy the equation 2x² + x - 300 = 0 which is a quadratic equation.

In this chapter, you will study quadratic equations, and various ways of finding their roots. You will also see some applications of quadratic equations in daily life situations.

content.text: Many people believe that Babylonians were the first to solve quadratic equations. For instance, they knew how to find two positive numbers with a given positive sum and a given positive product, and this problem is equivalent to solving a quadratic equation of the form x² - px + q = 0. Greek mathematician Euclid developed a geometrical approach for finding out lengths which, in our present day terminology, are solutions of quadratic equations. Solving of quadratic equations, in general form, is often credited to ancient Indian mathematicians. In fact, Brahmagupta (C.E.598-665) gave an explicit formula to solve a quadratic equation of the form ax² + bx = c. Later, Sridharacharya (C.E. 1025) derived a formula, now known as the quadratic formula, (as quoted by Bhaskara II) for solving a quadratic equation by the method of completing the square. An Arab mathematician Al-Khwarizmi (about C.E. 800) also studied quadratic equations of different types. Abraham bar Hiyya Ha-Nasi, in his book 'Liber embadorum' published in Europe in C.E. 1145 gave complete solutions of different quadratic equations.

content.text:
A quadratic equation in the variable x is an equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers, a ≠ 0. For example, 2x² + x - 300 = 0 is a quadratic equation. Similarly, 2x² - 3x + 1 = 0, 4x - 3x² + 2 = 0 and 1 - x² + 300 = 0 are also quadratic equations.
In fact, any equation of the form p(x) = 0, where p(x) is a polynomial of degree 2, is a quadratic equation. But when we write the terms of p(x) in descending order of their degrees, then we get the standard form of the equation. That is, ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0 is called the standard form of a quadratic equation.
Quadratic equations arise in several situations in the world around us and in different fields of mathematics. Let us consider a few examples.

content.text:
(i) Let the number of marbles John had be x.
Then the number of marbles Jivanti had = 45 - x (Why?).
The number of marbles left with John, when he lost 5 marbles = x - 5
The number of marbles left with Jivanti, when she lost 5 marbles = 45 - x - 5 = 40 - x
Therefore, their product = (x - 5) (40 - x)
= 40x - x² - 200 + 5x
= - x² + 45x - 200
So,    - x² + 45x - 200 = 124    (Given that product = 124)
i.e.,    - x² + 45x - 324 = 0
i.e.,    x² - 45x + 324 = 0
Therefore, the number of marbles John had, satisfies the quadratic equation
x² - 45x + 324 = 0
which is the required representation of the problem mathematically.

(ii) Let the number of toys produced on that day be x.
Therefore, the cost of production (in rupees) of each toy that day = 55 - x
So, the total cost of production (in rupees) that day = x (55 - x)
Therefore,    x (55 - x) = 750
i.e.,    55x - x² = 750
i.e.,    - x² + 55x - 750 = 0
i.e.,    x² - 55x + 750 = 0
Therefore, the number of toys produced that day satisfies the quadratic equation
x² - 55x + 750 = 0
which is the required representation of the problem mathematically.

content.text:
(i) LHS = (x - 2)² + 1 = x² - 4x + 4 + 1 = x² - 4x + 5
Therefore, (x - 2)² + 1 = 2x - 3 can be rewritten as
x² - 4x + 5 = 2x - 3
i.e.,    x² - 6x + 8 = 0
It is of the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
Therefore, the given equation is a quadratic equation.

(ii) Since x(x + 1) + 8 = x² + x + 8 and (x + 2)(x - 2) = x² - 4
Therefore,    x² + x + 8 = x² - 4
i.e.,    x + 12 = 0
It is not of the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
Therefore, the given equation is not a quadratic equation.

(iii) Here,    LHS = x (2x + 3) = 2x² + 3x
So, x (2x + 3) = x² + 1 can be rewritten as
2x² + 3x = x² + 1
Therefore, we get    x² + 3x - 1 = 0
It is of the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
So, the given equation is a quadratic equation.

(iv) Here,    LHS = (x + 2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8
Therefore, (x + 2)³ = x³ - 4 can be rewritten as
x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8 = x³ - 4
i.e.,    6x² + 12x + 12 = 0
or,    x² + 2x + 2 = 0
It is of the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
So, the given equation is a quadratic equation.

media.title: Roots and Zeroes: Why They Are the Same Values
media.description: A 2D whiteboard animation opens with the polynomial 2x² − 3x + 1 written in Navy Blue. A substitution panel appears beside it: x = 1 is entered in Orange and the arithmetic 2(1)² − 3(1) + 1 = 0 is computed step by step with each operation appearing individually. A dividing line then separates the screen into two panels: the left shows the polynomial labelled 'zero of the polynomial' and the right shows 2x² − 3x + 1 = 0 with the same x = 1 labelled 'root of the equation'. The two panels merge with an equals sign. A number-line segment appears below showing x = 1/2 and x = 1 marked with dots, labelled as the two roots, with the equation displayed above.
media.teaching_notes: WHEN to play: Play BEFORE students encounter the splitting method in T5, to ensure the concept of a root as a verifiable value is firmly established. WHAT to pause at: Pause at 55s before the split-panel appears and ask 'In your own words, what is the difference between a zero of a polynomial and a root of an equation?' WHAT to ask: After the video, ask 'If x = 1/2 is a root of 2x² − 3x + 1 = 0, what is the value of 2(1/2)² − 3(1/2) + 1? Show the arithmetic.'

content.text:
Consider the quadratic equation 2x² - 3x + 1 = 0. If we replace x by 1 on the LHS of this equation, we get (2 × 1²) - (3 × 1) + 1 = 0 = RHS of the equation. We say that 1 is a root of the quadratic equation 2x² - 3x + 1 = 0. This also means that 1 is a zero of the quadratic polynomial 2x² - 3x + 1.
In general, a real number α is called a root of the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0 if aα² + bα + c = 0. We also say that x = α is a solution of the quadratic equation, or that α satisfies the quadratic equation. Note that the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial ax² + bx + c and the roots of the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 are the same.
You have observed earlier that a quadratic polynomial can have at most two zeroes. So, any quadratic equation can have atmost two roots.

content.publication_text: Find the roots of the equation 2x² - 5x + 3 = 0, by factorisation.

content.text:
Let us first split the middle term - 5x as -2x -3x [because (-2x) × (-3x) = 6x² = (2x²) × 3].
So,    2x² - 5x + 3 = 2x² - 2x - 3x + 3 = 2x (x - 1) -3(x - 1) = (2x - 3)(x - 1)
Now, 2x² - 5x + 3 = 0 can be rewritten as (2x - 3)(x - 1) = 0.
So, the values of x for which 2x² - 5x + 3 = 0 are the same for which (2x - 3)(x - 1) = 0, i.e., either 2x - 3 = 0 or x - 1 = 0.
Now, 2x - 3 = 0 gives x = 3/2 and x - 1 = 0 gives x = 1.
So, x = 3/2 and x = 1 are the solutions of the equation.
In other words, 1 and 3/2 are the roots of the equation 2x² - 5x + 3 = 0.
Verify that these are the roots of the given equation.

Earlier, we found that if the breadth of the hall is x m, then x satisfies the equation 2x² + x - 300 = 0. Applying the factorisation method, we write this equation as
2x² - 24x + 25x - 300 = 0
2x (x - 12) + 25 (x - 12) = 0

So, the roots of the given equation are x = 12 or x = - 12.5. Since x is the breadth of the hall, it cannot be negative.
Thus, the breadth of the hall is 12 m. Its length = 2x + 1 = 25 m.

content.text:
If b² - 4ac > 0, we get two distinct real roots -b/2a + √(b² - 4ac)/2a and -b/2a - √(b² - 4ac)/2a.
If b² - 4ac = 0, then x = -b/2a ± 0, i.e., x = -b/2a or -b/2a.
So, the roots of the equation ax² + bx + c = 0 are both -b/2a.
Therefore, we say that the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 has two equal real roots in this case.
If b² - 4ac < 0, then there is no real number whose square is b² - 4ac. Therefore, there are no real roots for the given quadratic equation in this case.
Since b² - 4ac determines whether the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 has real roots or not, b² - 4ac is called the discriminant of this quadratic equation.
Let us consider some examples.

content.publication_text: A pole has to be erected at a point on the boundary of a circular park of diameter 13 metres in such a way that the differences of its distances from two diametrically opposite fixed gates A and B on the boundary is 7 metres. Is it possible to do so? If yes, at what distances from the two gates should the pole be erected?

content.text:
Let us first draw the diagram.
Let P be the required location of the pole. Let the distance of the pole from the gate B be x m, i.e., BP = x m. Now the difference of the distances of the pole from the two gates = AP - BP (or, BP - AP) = 7 m. Therefore, AP = (x + 7) m.
Now, AB = 13m, and since AB is a diameter,
∠APB = 90°    (Why?)
Therefore,    AP² + PB² = AB²    (By Pythagoras theorem)
i.e.,    (x + 7)² + x² = 13²
i.e.,    x² + 14x + 49 + x² = 169
i.e.,    2x² + 14x - 120 = 0
So, the distance 'x' of the pole from gate B satisfies the equation
x² + 7x - 60 = 0
So, it would be possible to place the pole if this equation has real roots. To see if this is so or not, let us consider its discriminant. The discriminant is
b² - 4ac = 7² - 4 × 1 × (- 60) = 289 > 0.
So, the given quadratic equation has two real roots, and it is possible to erect the pole on the boundary of the park.
Solving the quadratic equation x² + 7x - 60 = 0, by the quadratic formula, we get
x = (-7 ± √289)/2 = (-7 ± 17)/2
Therefore, x = 5 or - 12.
Since x is the distance between the pole and the gate B, it must be positive. Therefore, x = - 12 will have to be ignored. So, x = 5.
Thus, the pole has to be erected on the boundary of the park at a distance of 5m from the gate B and 12m from the gate A.

In this chapter, you have studied the following points:
1. A quadratic equation in the variable x is of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a ≠ 0.
2. A real number α is said to be a root of the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0, if aα² + bα + c = 0. The zeroes of the quadratic polynomial ax² + bx + c and the roots of the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 are the same.
3. If we can factorise ax² + bx + c, a ≠ 0, into a product of two linear factors, then the roots of the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 can be found by equating each factor to zero.
4. Quadratic formula: The roots of a quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 are given by (-b ± √(b² - 4ac)) / 2a, provided b² - 4ac ≥ 0.
5. A quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 has
(i) two distinct real roots, if b² - 4ac > 0,
(ii) two equal roots (i.e., coincident roots), if b² - 4ac = 0, and
(iii) no real roots, if b² - 4ac < 0.

objectives.objective_text: State the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0), identify the coefficients a, b, and c for any equation presented in standard form, and rearrange equations not in standard form before identifying the coefficients.
Construct a quadratic equation in standard form from a word problem by defining a variable x, expressing all related quantities in terms of x, and writing the given constraint as a degree-2 equation.

Determine whether a given algebraic equation is quadratic by expanding all brackets, collecting like terms on one side, and verifying that the simplified equation has degree 2 with a non-zero coefficient for x².
Classify an equation as quadratic or not quadratic by expanding all brackets, bringing all terms to one side, simplifying, and checking whether the resulting coefficient of x² is non-zero.
Verify that the formed equation correctly models the original situation by confirming it simplifies to ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0 and checking the logic with a trial substitution where applicable.

Explain the definition of a root α of ax² + bx + c = 0 as a value satisfying aα² + bα + c = 0, state why the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial ax² + bx + c and the roots of the equation are identical values, and state that any quadratic equation has at most two roots.
State the factorisation method (factorise ax² + bx + c into two linear factors and equate each factor to zero) and predict the pair of numbers that splits the middle term of a given equation.

Solve quadratic equations by the middle-term splitting method - finding a pair p, q with p × q = a × c and p + q = b, rewriting bx as px + qx, grouping the four terms in pairs, factorising each pair, and equating each resulting linear factor to zero.

Construct and solve a quadratic equation arising from a geometric word problem using the factorisation method, and explicitly reject any root that violates the physical constraints of the original problem, such as a negative length.

Solve quadratic equations, including those with integer, √2 and fractional coefficients, by factorisation, identifying the split pair (product = a × c, sum = b) and equating each linear factor to zero.
Translate a word problem into a quadratic equation in standard form, solve it by factorisation, and verify that the accepted root satisfies the physical constraints of the problem.
State the quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a, define the discriminant D = b² − 4ac, and identify a, b, and c correctly (with signs) from any quadratic equation written in standard form.

Predict the nature of the roots from the value of the discriminant D - two distinct real roots when D > 0, two equal real roots when D = 0, and no real roots when D < 0 - without fully solving the equation.
Compute D = b² − 4ac for 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0, correctly carrying the sign b = −4 throughout the calculation, confirm that D = −8 < 0, and conclude that the equation has no real roots.

Construct the equation x² + 7x − 60 = 0 from the circular-park problem using the Pythagorean theorem (∠APB = 90° by the angle-in-semicircle property), confirm D > 0, and solve using the quadratic formula, retaining only the positive root x = 5.
Justify the rejection of x = −12 by citing that BP is a physical distance that must be positive, demonstrating how real-world constraints determine which algebraic root is valid.
Compute D = b² − 4ac for 3x² − 2x + 1/3 = 0 by recognising the cancellation 4 × 3 × (1/3) = 4, confirm D = 0, and calculate the repeated root as −b/2a = 1/3.
Calculate D = b² − 4ac for a quadratic equation, classify the nature of its roots using the three discriminant cases, and find the exact roots by the quadratic formula when real roots exist.
Calculate the value(s) of k for which a quadratic equation has two equal real roots by setting D = b² − 4ac = 0, solving for k, and rejecting any value of k that makes the leading coefficient zero.
Verify each accepted value of k by substituting into D = b² − 4ac and confirming D = 0, then state the corresponding repeated root.
Compute the discriminant of the quadratic equation formed from the conditions of a design or age problem to decide whether the described figure or situation can exist.
Justify, from the sign of the discriminant, whether a described situation is possible, and interpret D = 0 as exactly one possible design, citing the three discriminant cases.

Explain how the standard form, the meaning of a root, the factorisation method, the quadratic formula and the three discriminant cases connect into one framework for solving and analysing quadratic equations.

Distinguish between quadratic equations that are efficiently solved by factorisation - when D is a perfect square - and those requiring the quadratic formula - when D is irrational or factorisation is not obvious - using the discriminant as the decision criterion.

carried_over_topics.summary: A quadratic equation is defined as an equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0 where a, b, c are real numbers and a ≠ 0; this standard form labels a as the leading coefficient, b as the coefficient of x, and c as the constant term. To determine whether a given equation is quadratic, expand all brackets, bring all terms to one side, and collect like terms - only the simplified result reveals the true degree. For example, (x − 2)² + 1 = 2x − 3 simplifies to x² − 6x + 8 = 0 (quadratic), while x(x + 1) + 8 = (x + 2)(x − 2) simplifies to x + 12 = 0 (linear, not quadratic) because the x² terms cancel. This classification skill is used whenever an equation must be verified as quadratic before applying any solution method.

carried_over_topics.brief_summary: A quadratic equation in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) is identified by expanding all terms, collecting like terms, and confirming the simplified equation has degree 2 with a non-zero leading coefficient.
carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: In Chapter 2, you studied polynomials of degree 2 - quadratic polynomials of the form ax² + bx + c, where a ≠ 0. You found their zeroes and examined the relationship between those zeroes and the coefficients a, b, c. This chapter extends that foundation: when we set a quadratic polynomial equal to zero, the result is a quadratic equation. The central questions become - how do we find the roots systematically, and what can the structure of the equation tell us about the real-world situation it models?

CORE - The Standard Form:
A quadratic equation in the variable x is an equation of the form

    ax² + bx + c = 0,  where a, b, c are real numbers and a ≠ 0.

This is the standard form of a quadratic equation. Three numbers characterise every such equation: a is the coefficient of x² (called the leading coefficient), b is the coefficient of x, and c is the constant term. The condition a ≠ 0 is non-negotiable - if a were zero, the x² term would vanish, and the equation would be linear (degree 1), not quadratic (degree 2).

Note that b or c may equal zero, but a may never equal zero. For example, x² − 4 = 0 is quadratic (here b = 0, c = −4), and x² + 3x = 0 is quadratic (here c = 0), but 3x − 7 = 0 is not quadratic (a = 0 in this context).

Convention for this chapter: Throughout Chapter 4, x denotes the unknown quantity being solved for. The coefficients will always be identified as a (the leading coefficient, a ≠ 0), b (the coefficient of x), and c (the constant term), matching the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0.

Equations such as 2x² + x − 300 = 0, 2x² − 3x + 1 = 0, 4x − 3x² + 2 = 0, and 1 − x² + 300 = 0 are all quadratic equations - each can be rearranged into standard form with a non-zero coefficient for x².

Motivation - A Real Situation:
Suppose a charity trust plans to build a prayer hall with a carpet area of 300 m², where the length must be one metre more than twice the breadth. Letting x = the breadth in metres, the length is (2x + 1) metres, and the area condition gives:

    x × (2x + 1) = 300
    2x² + x = 300
    2x² + x − 300 = 0

Here a = 2, b = 1, c = −300. We cannot read off the value of x directly from the coefficients - we need a solution method. The factorisation method developed in Module 2 will solve this equation, and we will return to it in Example 6.

Historical Note: The story of quadratic equations spans more than three millennia. Babylonian mathematicians (around 2000 BCE) solved problems equivalent to x² − px + q = 0 geometrically, reasoning about areas and lengths. The Greek mathematician Euclid constructed lengths - in modern terms, roots of quadratic equations - using straightedge and compass. In India, Brahmagupta (C.E. 598-665) gave an explicit formula for equations of the form ax² + bx = c. Sridharacharya (C.E. 1025) derived the formula now known as the quadratic formula, subsequently quoted by Bhaskara II. The Arab mathematician Al-Khwarizmi (about C.E. 800) systematically classified and solved quadratic equations of different types. Abraham bar Hiyya Ha-Nasi compiled complete solutions in his book Liber embadorum, published in Europe in C.E. 1145. The methods you will learn in this chapter trace directly to those contributions.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - COMPLETE:
Example 1: Represent the following two situations mathematically as quadratic equations.

(i) John and Jivanti together have 45 marbles. Both of them lost 5 marbles each, and the product of the number of marbles they now have is 124. We would like to find out how many marbles they had to start with.

Step 1 - Define the variable:
    Let x = the number of marbles John originally had.
    Then the number Jivanti originally had = 45 − x.
    (Why 45 − x? Because together they have 45 marbles, so once John's share is x, Jivanti has the remainder.)

Step 2 - Apply the loss:
    After each loses 5 marbles: John now has (x − 5) and Jivanti now has (45 − x − 5) = (40 − x).

Step 3 - Translate the product condition:
    (x − 5)(40 − x) = 124

WHY THIS STEP? The problem states the product of the remaining counts equals 124. Expressing "product" algebraically means multiplying the two expressions together and setting the result equal to 124.

Step 4 - Expand:
    (x − 5)(40 − x) = 40x − x² − 200 + 5x = −x² + 45x − 200

Step 5 - Set equal to 124 and rearrange:
    −x² + 45x − 200 = 124
    −x² + 45x − 324 = 0
    i.e.,  x² − 45x + 324 = 0     [multiply both sides by −1]

carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
In Chapter 2, you have studied different types of polynomials. One type was the quadratic polynomial of the form ax² + bx + c, a ≠ 0. When we equate this polynomial to zero, we get a quadratic equation. Quadratic equations come up when we deal with many real-life situations. For instance, suppose a charity trust decides to build a prayer hall having a carpet area of 300 square metres with its length one metre more than twice its breadth. What should be the length and breadth of the hall?
Suppose the breadth of the hall is x metres. Then, its length should be (2x + 1) metres. We can depict this information pictorially as shown in Fig. 4.1.
Now,     area of the hall = (2x + 1). x m² = (2x² + x) m²
So,     2x² + x = 300     (Given)
Therefore,     2x² + x - 300 = 0
So, the breadth of the hall should satisfy the equation 2x² + x - 300 = 0 which is a quadratic equation.

Many people believe that Babylonians were the first to solve quadratic equations. For instance, they knew how to find two positive numbers with a given positive sum and a given positive product, and this problem is equivalent to solving a quadratic equation of the form x² - px + q = 0. Greek mathematician Euclid developed a geometrical approach for finding out lengths which, in our present day terminology, are solutions of quadratic equations. Solving of quadratic equations, in general form, is often credited to ancient Indian mathematicians. In fact, Brahmagupta (C.E.598-665) gave an explicit formula to solve a quadratic equation of the form ax² + bx = c. Later, Sridharacharya (C.E. 1025) derived a formula, now known as the quadratic formula, (as quoted by Bhaskara II) for solving a quadratic equation by the method of completing the square. An Arab mathematician Al-Khwarizmi (about C.E. 800) also studied quadratic equations of different types. Abraham bar Hiyya Ha-Nasi, in his book ‘Liber embadorum’ published in Europe in C.E. 1145 gave complete solutions of different quadratic equations.

In this chapter, you will study quadratic equations, and various ways of finding their roots. You will also see some applications of quadratic equations in daily life situations.

4.2 Quadratic Equations

A quadratic equation in the variable x is an equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers, a ≠ 0. For example, 2x² + x - 300 = 0 is a quadratic equation. Similarly, 2x² - 3x + 1 = 0, 4x - 3x² + 2 = 0 and 1 - x² + 300 = 0 are also quadratic equations.
In fact, any equation of the form p(x) = 0, where p(x) is a polynomial of degree 2, is a quadratic equation. But when we write the terms of p(x) in descending order of their degrees, then we get the standard form of the equation. That is, ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0 is called the standard form of a quadratic equation.
Quadratic equations arise in several situations in the world around us and in different fields of mathematics. Let us consider a few examples.

Example 1 : Represent the following situations mathematically:
(i) John and Jivanti together have 45 marbles. Both of them lost 5 marbles each, and the product of the number of marbles they now have is 124. We would like to find out how many marbles they had to start with.
(ii) A cottage industry produces a certain number of toys in a day. The cost of production of each toy (in rupees) was found to be 55 minus the number of toys produced in a day. On a particular day, the total cost of production was ₹ 750. We would like to find out the number of toys produced on that day.

Solution :
(i) Let the number of marbles John had be x.
Then the number of marbles Jivanti had = 45 - x (Why?).
The number of marbles left with John, when he lost 5 marbles = x - 5
The number of marbles left with Jivanti, when she lost 5 marbles = 45 - x - 5 = 40 - x
Therefore, their product = (x - 5) (40 - x)
= 40x - x² - 200 + 5x
= - x² + 45x - 200
So,     - x² + 45x - 200 = 124     (Given that product = 124)
i.e.,     - x² + 45x - 324 = 0
i.e.,     x² - 45x + 324 = 0
Therefore, the number of marbles John had, satisfies the quadratic equation
x² - 45x + 324 = 0
which is the required representation of the problem mathematically.

(ii) Let the number of toys produced on that day be x.
Therefore, the cost of production (in rupees) of each toy that day = 55 - x
So, the total cost of production (in rupees) that day = x (55 - x)
Therefore,     x (55 - x) = 750
i.e.,     55x - x² = 750
i.e.,     - x² + 55x - 750 = 0
i.e.,     x² - 55x + 750 = 0
Therefore, the number of toys produced that day satisfies the quadratic equation
x² - 55x + 750 = 0
which is the required representation of the problem mathematically.

Example 2 : Check whether the following are quadratic equations:
(i) (x - 2)² + 1 = 2x - 3
(ii) x(x + 1) + 8 = (x + 2) (x - 2)
(iii) x (2x + 3) = x² + 1
(iv) (x + 2)³ = x³ - 4

Solution :
(i) LHS = (x - 2)² + 1 = x² - 4x + 4 + 1 = x² - 4x + 5
Therefore, (x - 2)² + 1 = 2x - 3 can be rewritten as
x² - 4x + 5 = 2x - 3
i.e.,     x² - 6x + 8 = 0
It is of the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
Therefore, the given equation is a quadratic equation.

(ii) Since x(x + 1) + 8 = x² + x + 8 and (x + 2)(x - 2) = x² - 4
Therefore,     x² + x + 8 = x² - 4
i.e.,     x + 12 = 0
It is not of the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
Therefore, the given equation is not a quadratic equation.

(iii) Here, LHS = x (2x + 3) = 2x² + 3x
So, x (2x + 3) = x² + 1 can be rewritten as
2x² + 3x = x² + 1
Therefore, we get     x² + 3x - 1 = 0
It is of the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
So, the given equation is a quadratic equation.

(iv) Here, LHS = (x + 2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8
Therefore, (x + 2)³ = x³ - 4 can be rewritten as
x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8 = x³ - 4
i.e.,     6x² + 12x + 12 = 0   or,   x² + 2x + 2 = 0
It is of the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
So, the given equation is a quadratic equation.

Remark : Be careful! In (ii) above, the given equation appears to be a quadratic equation, but it is not a quadratic equation.
In (iv) above, the given equation appears to be a cubic equation (an equation of degree 3) and not a quadratic equation. But it turns out to be a quadratic equation. As you can see, often we need to simplify the given equation before deciding whether it is quadratic or not.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
CORE - Classification Strategy:
To determine whether a given equation is quadratic, follow a systematic procedure rather than inspecting it by eye.

Step 1: Expand all brackets completely on both sides of the equation.
Step 2: Bring all terms to one side so that the equation has the form "expression = 0".
Step 3: Collect like terms and simplify the expression.
Step 4: Examine the simplified expression. If its highest-degree term is x² and its coefficient is non-zero, the equation is quadratic. If the x² terms cancel (coefficient becomes zero), the equation is not quadratic.

This four-step procedure protects against the two most common errors: treating an equation as quadratic because x² appears somewhere in it, and dismissing an equation as non-quadratic because it appears to be of higher degree before simplification.

ERROR ALERT: Pay particular attention to equations of the form A(x) = B(x) where both A and B contain x². When you subtract B from both sides, the x² terms may cancel entirely, leaving a linear equation. Example: x(x + 2) = x(x − 5) simplifies to 2x = −5x → 7x = 0, which is linear, not quadratic.

CORE - The Translation Method:
Forming a quadratic equation from a word problem is a skill in itself, separate from solving the equation. It requires translating a verbal description into algebraic language through deliberate steps.

Step 1 (Define): Choose a variable - typically x - to represent the unknown quantity. Be specific: "let x = the breadth in metres" is better than "let x = the measurement".
Step 2 (Express): Write all other quantities mentioned in the problem in terms of x.
Step 3 (Equation): Identify the constraint or condition given in the problem and write it as an algebraic equation.
Step 4 (Expand and simplify): Expand the equation and rearrange it into standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0.
Step 5 (Check): Verify that the equation correctly encodes the original situation - substitute a trial value and confirm the logic holds.

APPLICATION SCAFFOLD - Problem (i):

THE PROBLEM: The area of a rectangular plot is 528 m². The length of the plot (in metres) is one more than twice its breadth.

WHAT'S THE SITUATION? A rectangle whose dimensions are linked by a specific rule, and whose area is known.

WHAT DO WE KNOW?
    • Area = 528 m²
    • Length = (2 × breadth) + 1 metres

WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND? The value of the breadth (and hence the length).

TRANSLATE TO MATHS:
    Let x = breadth in metres. Then length = (2x + 1) metres.
    Area = x(2x + 1) = 528
    2x² + x = 528
    2x² + x − 528 = 0

CHECK AGAINST THE SITUATION: Does this equation correctly encode the original problem? Setting x = 16 gives 2(256) + 16 − 528 = 512 + 16 − 528 = 0. So x = 16 is a root, corresponding to a breadth of 16 m and a length of 33 m, with area 16 × 33 = 528 m². The equation is correct.

For problems (ii)-(iv), apply the same five steps. The guidance below helps you set up each equation.

(ii) The product of two consecutive positive integers is 306.
    Let x = the smaller integer. Then the next consecutive integer = x + 1. The product condition gives x(x + 1) = 306. Expand and rearrange to standard form.

(iii) Rohan's mother is 26 years older than him. Three years from now, the product of their ages will be 360.
    Let x = Rohan's present age. His mother's present age = x + 26. Three years from now, their ages are (x + 3) and (x + 29). Set (x + 3)(x + 29) = 360 and simplify.

(iv) A train travels 480 km at a uniform speed. If the speed had been 8 km/h less, it would have taken 3 hours more.
    Let x = the actual speed of the train in km/h. Then time at speed x = 480/x hours, and time at speed (x − 8) = 480/(x − 8) hours. The difference in times is 3 hours. Cross-multiplying will produce a quadratic equation in x.

CORE - Definition of a Root:
A real number α is called a root of the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) if substituting x = α satisfies the equation:

    aα² + bα + c = 0.

We also say that x = α is a solution of the equation, or that α satisfies the equation. The words "root" and "solution" are used interchangeably throughout this chapter.

The direct connection to Chapter 2: the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial ax² + bx + c and the roots of the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 are identical values. The difference is perspective - "zeroes" describes the polynomial viewed as a function; "roots" describes the equation as a statement of equality.

To confirm that 1 is a root of 2x² − 3x + 1 = 0: substitute x = 1 on the LHS:
    2(1)² − 3(1) + 1 = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0 = RHS. ✓

How many roots can a quadratic equation have? In Chapter 2 you established that a quadratic polynomial can have at most two zeroes. It follows directly that any quadratic equation can have at most two roots. In practice, a quadratic equation can have exactly two distinct real roots, two equal (repeated) real roots, or no real roots at all - you will determine which case applies using the discriminant in Module 3.

You have learnt in Class IX how to factorise quadratic polynomials by splitting their middle terms. The next topic applies that skill to find the roots of quadratic equations systematically.

ERROR ALERT: A common confusion is treating the polynomial 2x² − 3x + 1 and the equation 2x² − 3x + 1 = 0 as interchangeable. The polynomial is an algebraic expression; the equation is a statement that the expression equals zero. Finding the roots means identifying which specific values of x make the equation true.

carried_over_topics.summary: The factorisation method exploits the zero-product property: if ax² + bx + c factors as (px + q)(rx + s), then the equation equals zero when either px + q = 0 or rx + s = 0, giving x = −q/p or x = −s/r. The key challenge is finding the split pair: two numbers p and q such that p × q = a × c and p + q = b - getting this reversed (product equals b, sum equals a × c) is the most frequent error. For example, 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0 has a × c = 6, and the split pair −2 and −3 satisfies (−2)(−3) = 6 and (−2) + (−3) = −5, leading to the factorisation (2x − 3)(x − 1) = 0 with roots x = 3/2 and x = 1. The method applies equally to equations with irrational coefficients: 3x² − 2√6 x + 2 = 0 splits with −√6 and −√6, yielding the repeated root √(2/3).

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
CORE - The Splitting Method:
In Chapter 2, you learnt to factorise quadratic polynomials by splitting the middle term. That technique now directly solves quadratic equations. The central insight: if ax² + bx + c factors as (px + q)(rx + s), then the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 are obtained by setting each linear factor to zero:

    px + q = 0  →  x = −q/p
    rx + s = 0  →  x = −s/r

The challenge is finding the correct factorisation. Here is the systematic procedure to split the middle term bx of ax² + bx + c:

    Step 1: Compute the product a × c.
    Step 2: Find two numbers p and q such that p × q = a × c and p + q = b.
    Step 3: Rewrite bx as px + qx.
    Step 4: Group the four terms in pairs and factorise each group.
    Step 5: Extract the common linear factor and write the product of two linear factors.
    Step 6: Set each factor to zero and solve for x.

Convention: Throughout this chapter, when the splitting method is applied, the two numbers found in Step 2 will be called the split pair. Their product must equal a × c (not b), and their sum must equal b (not a × c).

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 - COMPLETE:
Example 3: Find the roots of the equation 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0 by factorisation.

Step 1: a = 2, b = −5, c = 3.  Compute a × c = 2 × 3 = 6.
Step 2: Find the split pair: two numbers whose product is 6 and whose sum is −5. Those numbers are −2 and −3.  (Check: (−2) × (−3) = 6 ✓;  (−2) + (−3) = −5 ✓.)
Step 3: Split the middle term: 2x² − 5x + 3 = 2x² − 2x − 3x + 3.

WHY THIS STEP? Replacing −5x with −2x + (−3x) does not change the expression (since −2 + (−3) = −5), but splitting allows us to group consecutive pairs in the next step.

Step 4: Group and factorise:
    2x² − 2x − 3x + 3
    = 2x(x − 1) − 3(x − 1)
    = (2x − 3)(x − 1)

WHY THIS STEP? We factored out 2x from the first pair and −3 from the second pair, revealing the common factor (x − 1). Factoring (x − 1) out gives two linear factors.

Step 5: The equation 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0 becomes (2x − 3)(x − 1) = 0.
Step 6: Set each factor to zero:
    2x − 3 = 0  →  x = 3/2
    x − 1 = 0   →  x = 1

The roots of 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0 are x = 3/2 and x = 1.

Verification: Substituting x = 1: 2(1) − 5(1) + 3 = 0 ✓.  Substituting x = 3/2: 2(9/4) − 5(3/2) + 3 = 9/2 − 15/2 + 6/2 = 0 ✓.

Note: The roots were found by factorising 2x² − 5x + 3 into two linear factors and equating each factor to zero.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 - PARTIALLY FADED:
Example 4: Find the roots of the quadratic equation 6x² − x − 2 = 0.

Step 1: a = 6, b = −1, c = −2.  Compute a × c = 6 × (−2) = −12.
Step 2: Find the split pair: two numbers with product −12 and sum −1.  Those numbers are 3 and −4.  (Check: 3 × (−4) = −12 ✓;  3 + (−4) = −1 ✓.)
Step 3: Split the middle term:
    6x² − x − 2 = 6x² + 3x − 4x − 2
Step 4: Group and factorise:
    = 3x(2x + 1) − 2(2x + 1)
Now complete the factorisation. The common factor in both groups is (2x + 1). Extract it and write the equation as a product of two linear factors, then find both roots.

carried_over_topics.original_chunk:
Example 3 : Find the roots of the equation 2x² - 5x + 3 = 0, by factorisation.
Solution : Let us first split the middle term - 5x as -2x -3x [because (-2x) × (-3x) = 6x² = (2x²) × 3].
So, 2x² - 5x + 3 = 2x² - 2x - 3x + 3 = 2x (x - 1) -3(x - 1) = (2x - 3)(x - 1)
Now, 2x² - 5x + 3 = 0 can be rewritten as (2x - 3)(x - 1) = 0.
So, the values of x for which 2x² - 5x + 3 = 0 are the same for which (2x - 3)(x - 1) = 0, i.e., either 2x - 3 = 0 or x - 1 = 0.
Now, 2x - 3 = 0 gives x = 3/2 and x - 1 = 0 gives x = 1.
So, x = 3/2 and x = 1 are the solutions of the equation.
In other words, 1 and 3/2 are the roots of the equation 2x² - 5x + 3 = 0.
Verify that these are the roots of the given equation.

Note that we have found the roots of 2x² - 5x + 3 = 0 by factorising 2x² - 5x + 3 into two linear factors and equating each factor to zero.

Example 4 : Find the roots of the quadratic equation 6x² - x - 2 = 0.
Solution : We have
6x² - x - 2 = 6x² + 3x - 4x - 2
= 3x (2x + 1) - 2 (2x + 1)
= (3x - 2)(2x + 1)
The roots of 6x² - x - 2 = 0 are the values of x for which (3x - 2)(2x + 1) = 0
Therefore, 3x - 2 = 0 or 2x + 1 = 0,
i.e.,     x = 2/3   or   x = -1/2
Therefore, the roots of 6x² - x - 2 = 0 are 2/3 and -1/2.
We verify the roots, by checking that 2/3 and -1/2 satisfy 6x² - x - 2 = 0.

Example 5 : Find the roots of the quadratic equation 3x² - 2√6x + 2 = 0.
Solution : 3x² - 2√6x + 2 = 3x² - √6x - √6x + 2
= √3x(√3x - √2) - √2(√3x - √2)
= (√3x - √2)(√3x - √2)
So, the roots of the equation are the values of x for which
(√3x - √2)(√3x - √2) = 0
Now, √3x - √2 = 0 for x = √(2/3).
So, this root is repeated twice, one for each repeated factor √3x - √2.
Therefore, the roots of 3x² - 2√6x + 2 = 0 are √(2/3), √(2/3).
concept_bullets: The split pair must satisfy product = a × c and sum = b - for example, for 6x² − x − 2 = 0, a × c = −12 and b = −1, so the pair is 3 and −4 since 3 × (−4) = −12 and 3 + (−4) = −1.
After splitting, group consecutive pairs and factor out the common monomial from each - for example, 2x² − 2x − 3x + 3 groups as 2x(x − 1) − 3(x − 1), revealing the common factor (x − 1).
The zero-product property gives the roots: if (2x − 3)(x − 1) = 0, then either 2x − 3 = 0 giving x = 3/2, or x − 1 = 0 giving x = 1.
When the split pair consists of two equal irrational numbers, the equation has a repeated root - for example, 3x² − 2√6 x + 2 = 0 splits as (−√6)(−√6) = 6, yielding the double root x = √(2/3).
carried_over_topics.detailed_summary: The factorisation method exploits the zero-product property: if ax² + bx + c factors as (px + q)(rx + s), then the equation equals zero when either px + q = 0 or rx + s = 0, giving x = −q/p or x = −s/r. The key challenge is finding the split pair: two numbers p and q such that p × q = a × c and p + q = b - getting this reversed (product equals b, sum equals a × c) is the most frequent error. For example, 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0 has a × c = 6, and the split pair −2 and −3 satisfies (−2)(−3) = 6 and (−2) + (−3) = −5, leading to the factorisation (2x − 3)(x − 1) = 0 with roots x = 3/2 and x = 1. The method applies equally to equations with irrational coefficients: 3x² − 2√6 x + 2 = 0 splits with −√6 and −√6, yielding the repeated root √(2/3).
important_points: Now, 2x² - 5x + 3 = 0 can be rewritten as (2x - 3)(x - 1) = 0.
x = 3/2 and x = 1 are the solutions of the equation.
the roots of 6x² - x - 2 = 0 are 2/3 and -1/2.
the roots of 3x² - 2√6x + 2 = 0 are √(2/3), √(2/3).

recall_questions.answer: The split pair p and q must satisfy two conditions: (1) p × q = a × c (the product of the split numbers equals the product of the leading coefficient and the constant term), and (2) p + q = b (the sum of the split numbers equals the coefficient of the middle term). Condition (1) is necessary to ensure that when we rewrite bx as px + qx and group in pairs, the common factor extraction remains valid. Condition (2) ensures that replacing bx with px + qx does not change the value of the expression, since p + q = b means the total coefficient of x is unchanged.

APPLICATION - Example 6: Finding the Dimensions of the Prayer Hall

THE PROBLEM: Find the actual length and breadth of the prayer hall introduced in Section 4.1.

WHAT'S THE SITUATION? In Topic T1 (Section 4.1), we established that if the breadth of the hall is x metres, then the length is (2x + 1) metres and the area equals 300 m². The translation step has already been completed, giving the equation:

    2x² + x − 300 = 0

WHAT DO WE KNOW?
    • Breadth = x metres
    • Length = (2x + 1) metres
    • Equation: 2x² + x − 300 = 0, with a = 2, b = 1, c = −300.

WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND? The value of x (the breadth), from which the length follows immediately.

SOLVE - Factorisation:
Applying the splitting method established in Topic T5:

Step 1: Compute a × c = 2 × (−300) = −600.
Step 2: Find the split pair: two numbers with product −600 and sum 1.
    Those numbers are 25 and −24.  (Check: 25 × (−24) = −600 ✓;  25 + (−24) = 1 ✓.)
Step 3: Split the middle term:
    2x² + x − 300 = 2x² − 24x + 25x − 300
Step 4: Group and factorise:
    = 2x(x − 12) + 25(x − 12)
    = (x − 12)(2x + 25)
Step 5: Set each factor to zero:
    x − 12 = 0   →  x = 12
    2x + 25 = 0  →  x = −12.5

CHECK AGAINST THE SITUATION: The breadth of a physical hall must be a positive length; x = −12.5 is not physically valid and is rejected. The valid root is x = 12.

Therefore:
    Breadth = 12 m
    Length = 2(12) + 1 = 25 m

Verify: Area = 12 × 25 = 300 m² ✓. Length is indeed one more than twice the breadth: 2(12) + 1 = 25 ✓.

Connection (EX2): A similar approach resolves the room-dimensions problem from EX2: a rectangular room in Ahmedabad has an area of 66 m², with the length 5 metres more than the breadth. Letting x = breadth gives x(x + 5) = 66, i.e., x² + 5x − 66 = 0. The split pair for a × c = −66 and sum = 5 is 11 and −6, giving (x + 11)(x − 6) = 0 → breadth = 6 m, length = 11 m. Notice that in both cases, the factorisation produces one positive and one negative root, and physical context selects the positive root.

ERROR ALERT: When a quadratic equation yields two roots, both roots must be tested against the physical constraints of the original problem before accepting an answer. In applied geometry and measurement problems, negative values almost always represent physically invalid solutions and must be rejected explicitly - not silently discarded.

CHECK: Suppose the prayer hall were required to have an area of 150 m² (with the same condition that length = 2 × breadth + 1). Write the new quadratic equation and solve it by factorisation. State which root is physically valid and give the dimensions.

STRATEGY OVERVIEW - Exercise 4.2:
This exercise builds fluency with the factorisation method across a wider range of quadratic equations: Q1 includes equations with integer, irrational (√2), and fractional coefficients; Q2 returns to the word-problem equations formed in Example 1; and Q3-Q6 require you to first translate a situation into an equation (as in Exercise 4.1 Q2) before solving.

For Q1 - direct factorisation: apply the six-step splitting procedure from Topic T5 to each equation. For each, compute a × c, find the split pair (product = a × c, sum = b), split the middle term, group and factorise, then set each linear factor to zero. The equations in parts (iii)-(v) involve irrational or fractional coefficients; the same procedure applies - take care with arithmetic when computing the split pair.

For Q2 - solving Example 1's equations: the equations x² − 45x + 324 = 0 and x² − 55x + 750 = 0 were formed in Example 1 (Topic T1). Now apply factorisation to find the roots. After finding the roots, interpret them in the context of the original problem - check that the solutions are positive integers and make physical sense.

For Q3-Q6 - word problems: begin by translating each situation into a quadratic equation using the five-step translation method from Topic T3 (define the variable, express related quantities, write the condition, expand, rearrange to standard form). Then solve by factorisation. Finally, check each root against the physical constraints of the problem.

EXERCISE 4.2
1. Find the roots of the following quadratic equations by factorisation:
(i) x² - 3x - 10 = 0
(ii) 2x² + x - 6 = 0
(iii) √2 x² + 7x + 5√2 = 0
(iv) 2x² - x + 1/8 = 0

Step 2 - Write the constraint: x² + (x + 1)² = 365.

carried_over_topics.summary: When factorisation is impractical - for example, when the split pair involves irrational values - the quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a gives the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 directly. The expression D = b² − 4ac is called the discriminant because its sign discriminates among the three possible root types: D > 0 gives two distinct real roots (−b ± √D) / 2a; D = 0 gives two equal real roots both equal to −b / 2a; and D < 0 means no real roots exist because √D would require the square root of a negative number. For example, for x² + 7x − 60 = 0, computing D = 49 + 240 = 289 > 0 immediately confirms two distinct real roots without full solving. The sign of b in the formula must be read from the standard form - for 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0, b = −4 not +4.

carried_over_topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: The factorisation method in Module 2 required finding a split pair - two numbers whose product equals a × c and whose sum equals b. For many equations, such as x² − 7x + 12 = 0, this works efficiently. However, for equations where the split pair involves irrational or non-integer values - for example, x² + 7x − 60 = 0 or 3x² − 2x + 1/3 = 0 - identifying the split pair by inspection is impractical. The quadratic formula provides a direct path to the roots of any quadratic equation, without requiring factorisation.

CORE - The Quadratic Formula:
The roots of the equation ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) are given by:

    x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a

Here a, b, c are the coefficients in the standard form established in Topic T1: a is the coefficient of x² (a ≠ 0), b is the coefficient of x (carries its sign), and c is the constant term.

The expression b² − 4ac, which appears under the square root, is called the discriminant of the quadratic equation. It is denoted by D:

    D = b² − 4ac

The discriminant determines the nature of the roots - that is, how many real roots the equation has and whether they are equal or distinct - without requiring a complete solution.

The three cases are:
(i)   If D > 0: the equation has two distinct real roots,
          x = (−b + √D) / 2a   and   x = (−b − √D) / 2a.
(ii)  If D = 0: the equation has two equal real roots, both equal to −b / 2a.
(iii) If D < 0: the equation has no real roots. Since D is negative, √D is not a real number, and neither root formula yields a real value.

In summary, a quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0 has:
(i)   two distinct real roots,   if b² − 4ac > 0,
(ii)  two equal real roots,      if b² − 4ac = 0,
(iii) no real roots,             if b² − 4ac < 0.

These three cases are illustrated in Examples 7, 8, and 9 in the topics that follow.

ERROR ALERT: When substituting into the quadratic formula, b is the coefficient of x and carries its sign from the equation. For 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0, the value is b = −4, not b = 4. Substituting b = +4 changes both the discriminant calculation and the formula output, producing entirely wrong roots. Always read b directly from the standard form - its sign is part of its value.
